statements.status_notes: MariaDB Connector/J checked a server's LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE file request by searching the command it had sent for LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '<file>'. The search also matched inside quoted identifiers, string literals and comments, so an identifier returned by the server and re-used in a later query, for example by DatabaseMetaData.getImportedKeys(), getExportedKeys() or updatable result sets, could satisfy it. A rogue or machine-in-the-middle server can read any file the client JVM can read. This issue is fixed in versions 3.3.7, 3.4.5, and 3.5.11.
statements.action_statement: Upgrade to Liquibase Secure 6.0.1 or later, which bundles mariadb-java-client 3.5.11. Liquibase Secure 5.0.0 through 6.0.0 bundle 3.5.6 to 3.5.10, which are affected. Liquibase never sets allowLocalInfile, so the driver default (true) applies. Commands that read foreign key metadata from a MariaDB connection (snapshot, diff, diff-changelog, generate-changelog, and foreignKeyConstraintExists preconditions) can call DatabaseMetaData.getImportedKeys() with table names returned by the server: the core snapshot does so directly, and the Pro bulk foreign key query falls back to it whenever the bulk query fails, which the server controls. A malicious or compromised MariaDB server, or a machine-in-the-middle on a connection without verified TLS (the driver default), can therefore read any file the Liquibase process can read, such as liquibase.properties, credential files and key stores, without any visible error.

statements.status_notes: MariaDB Connector/J sized heap allocations from lengths declared by the server in OK packets before checking that those lengths fit in the packet. When CLIENT_SESSION_TRACK is negotiated (the default), a rogue or machine-in-the-middle server can make the client allocate megabytes from a packet of a few bytes, creating GC pressure up to OutOfMemoryError. This issue is fixed in versions 3.3.7, 3.4.5, and 3.5.11.
statements.impact_statement: The oversized allocations are driven by lengths in OK packets sent by the server, so exploitation requires a malicious or compromised MariaDB server, or a machine-in-the-middle, on the connection Liquibase opened. The only impact is an OutOfMemoryError that ends the Liquibase process. Liquibase is a short-lived command-line client, and an attacker in that position can already stop the run by refusing or dropping the connection, so the flaw gives no capability beyond what control of the connection already does. Liquibase Secure 5.0.0 through 6.0.0 bundle mariadb-java-client 3.5.6 to 3.5.10; Liquibase Secure 6.0.1 and later bundle 3.5.11, which includes the fix.

statements.status_notes: MariaDB Connector/J is used to connect applications developed in Java to MariaDB and MySQL databases. From 3.0.0 until 3.3.7, 3.4.5, and 3.5.10, the ReadableByteBuf.readLength() and ReadableByteBuf.readIntLengthEncodedNotNull() methods narrowed the protocol's unsigned 8-byte length-encoded integer to a Java int without checking that the value fit a non-negative integer. Values above Integer.MAX_VALUE could wrap to a negative or unrelated length that downstream allocation and read paths used. A malicious or compromised server, or a machine-in-the-middle attacker, could trigger NegativeArraySizeException, out-of-bounds failures, or oversized allocation behavior in client connection handling. This issue is fixed in versions 3.3.7, 3.4.5, and 3.5.10.
statements.impact_statement: The truncated lengths come from length-encoded integers in packets sent by the server, so exploitation requires a malicious or compromised MariaDB server, or a machine-in-the-middle, on the connection Liquibase opened. The only impact is an unchecked exception (NegativeArraySizeException, an out-of-bounds error) or an oversized allocation that ends the current Liquibase command. Liquibase is a short-lived command-line client, and an attacker in that position can already stop the run by refusing or dropping the connection, so the flaw gives no capability beyond what control of the connection already does. Liquibase Secure 5.0.0 through 5.2.2 bundle mariadb-java-client 3.5.6 to 3.5.9, which are in the affected range; Liquibase Secure 6.0.0 bundles 3.5.10, which includes the fix.

statements.status_notes: MariaDB Connector/J is used to connect applications developed in Java to MariaDB and MySQL databases. From 3.0.0 until 3.3.7, 3.4.5, and 3.5.11, the MariaDbPoolConnection.recover() and MariaDbPoolPinnedConnection.recover() implementations trusted the gtrid_length and bqual_length columns returned by XA RECOVER. The methods allocated and split Xid byte arrays without validating the lengths against Xid.MAXGTRIDSIZE, Xid.MAXBQUALSIZE, or the actual data payload. A malicious or compromised server, or a machine-in-the-middle attacker, could cause large allocations, NegativeArraySizeException, or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException during XA recovery. This issue is fixed in versions 3.3.7, 3.4.5, and 3.5.11.
statements.impact_statement: The flaw is in XAResource.recover() of MariaDbPoolConnection and MariaDbPoolPinnedConnection, which a distributed transaction manager calls during XA recovery. Liquibase Secure opens database connections through java.sql.Driver.connect() only. It never requests an XA or pooled connection (getXAConnection, getPooledConnection), never uses XAResource or the javax.transaction.xa API, and never issues XA RECOVER, so the vulnerable recovery code never runs. Liquibase Secure 5.0.0 through 6.0.0 bundle mariadb-java-client 3.5.6 to 3.5.10; Liquibase Secure 6.0.1 and later bundle 3.5.11, which includes the fix.

statements.status_notes: MariaDB Connector/J decodes every result as UTF-8 and guards character_set_client against a change to another charset, but did not guard character_set_results, and relied on the server's global session_track_system_variables list to be told about charset changes. A malicious or compromised server, or a machine-in-the-middle, could make the strings an application reads differ from the bytes the server returned, which can defeat application-side validation or escaping built on those values. This issue is fixed in versions 3.3.7, 3.4.5, and 3.5.11.
statements.impact_statement: Exploitation requires a malicious or compromised MariaDB server, or a machine-in-the-middle, that switches character_set_results on the connection Liquibase opened. The effect is that strings Liquibase reads differ from the bytes the server sent. Liquibase does not rely on decoding of server results for validation or escaping: the values it reads (DATABASECHANGELOG rows, snapshot metadata) come from that same server, which can already return any value it chooses, so the charset switch gives no capability beyond what control of the connection already does. Liquibase Secure 5.0.0 through 6.0.0 bundle mariadb-java-client 3.5.6 to 3.5.10; Liquibase Secure 6.0.1 and later bundle 3.5.11, which includes the fix.

statements.status_notes: When an application connects with sslMode=verify-full or verify-ca and a password but does not pin a server certificate, Connector/J accepts an untrusted certificate at the TLS layer and proves the server's identity afterwards by binding the certificate fingerprint into the authentication exchange. That check is not applied on the initial-handshake path, so an active man-in-the-middle that names the mysql_clear_password plugin receives the password in cleartext before any identity check runs.
statements.impact_statement: Fixed in mariadb-java-client 3.5.9. Liquibase Secure 5.2.2 and later ship 3.5.9 or newer, which includes the fix. Releases 5.0.0 through 5.2.1 shipped 3.5.6 or 3.5.7 and are affected.

statements.status_notes: When PAM (dialog) authentication is used, the connector can be coerced into sending the account password in cleartext over an insecure connection. A hostile or man-in-the-middle server can trigger this with the default configuration by issuing an Authentication Switch Request for the dialog plugin over plain TCP.
statements.impact_statement: Fixed in mariadb-java-client 3.5.9. Liquibase Secure 5.2.2 and later ship 3.5.9 or newer, which includes the fix. Releases 5.0.0 through 5.2.1 shipped 3.5.6 or 3.5.7 and are affected.

statements.status_notes: The connector encodes and decodes all character data assuming the connection character set is UTF-8. A server can change character_set_client mid-session to a non-UTF-8 charset, after which the driver and server interpret the same bytes under different encodings. This causes silent data corruption and is a primitive that can defeat byte-wise quoting and escaping.
statements.impact_statement: Fixed in mariadb-java-client 3.5.9. Liquibase Secure 5.2.2 and later ship 3.5.9 or newer, which includes the fix. Releases 5.0.0 through 5.2.1 shipped 3.5.6 or 3.5.7 and are affected.

statements.status_notes: MariaDB Connector/J does not enforce allowLocalInfile=false when a server answers a query with a LOCAL INFILE request. When a client runs LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE, a rogue or man-in-the-middle server can echo the same filename back and the connector sends the file content even though local infile was disabled. The server cannot redirect the request to a different file than the one named in the client's query.
statements.impact_statement: Fixed in mariadb-java-client 3.5.9. Liquibase Secure 5.2.2 and later ship 3.5.9 or newer, which includes the fix. Releases 5.0.0 through 5.2.1 shipped 3.5.6 or 3.5.7 and are affected. Liquibase never sets allowLocalInfile and never issues LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE itself (the loadData change type sends INSERT statements), so exposure on those releases requires a user who sets allowLocalInfile=false in the JDBC URL, runs LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE in changelog SQL, and connects to a rogue or man-in-the-middle server. With the driver default (allowLocalInfile=true) the fixed and unfixed drivers behave the same.
